Build a Model Specification

Source: R/spec.R
statmod_spec.Rd

Builds everything from which statmod() fits: splits the formula into one equation per distribution parameter, interprets each with modelterms7, and builds the terms that it names against the data. statmod() calls this first, and calling it directly inspects a model without fitting it.

Usage

statmod_spec(
  formula,
  distrib,
  data,
  weights = NULL,
  offsets = NULL,
  need_response = TRUE,
  linpar = list()
)

Arguments

formula

The model formula, with the parameters' equations separated by |.

distrib

A distributions7 distribution object, which determines how many equations there are and what they are called.

data

A data frame holding the response, the covariates and any matrix columns that the terms name. A missing value in the response, or in a variable that an equation names, is an error, because a fit does not drop rows.

weights

Optional prior weights, a numeric vector of length nrow(data) (not the name of a column), or NULL for all ones. The weights must be non-negative, finite and complete, and not all zero. They act as frequency weights and are not normalized.

offsets

Optional named list of offsets, one entry per parameter, each a finite numeric vector of length 1 or nrow(data), summed with any offset the formula names for the same parameter.

need_response

TRUE, the default, requires the left-hand side to evaluate. Prediction uses FALSE, because new data routinely has no response column.

linpar

How the implicit parametric block is built, as linpar_options() returns it. The options are kept on the specification, so that a rebuild such as a fold of cv() reproduces the storage instead of quietly densifying.

Value

A StatmodSpec() object.

The formula

The equations are separated by |, and the first of them carries the response. A parameter with no equation is given an intercept. statmod_equations() does the split, which is not the obvious one: R's precedence reduces the whole right-hand side of a three-equation formula to the last term.

Each equation is interpreted in an environment where modelterms7's term constructors sit in front of the search path, so s() means this toolkit's even with mgcv attached.

Rejected before any fit

The function signals an error for a multivariate family (which distributions7::fit_distrib() fits with constant parameters), a censored response written with cens(), a family method whose signature has no ..., a missing value in the response or in a variable that an equation names, a two-column response on a family without size, an offset written inside another term, and a structural term that cannot be fitted or a formula with more than one structural term.

Prior weights are not normalized

They enter the log-likelihood as \(\sum_i w_i \ell_i\) and are taken as given, so they act as frequency weights: a constant weight \(c\) on every row is \(c\) copies of the data. Dividing the weights by their sum would turn the log-likelihood into a mean, multiplying every standard error by \(\sqrt{n}\) and making the information criteria incomparable with an unweighted fit of the same model.

The restricted (REML) criterion counts \(c n\) observations against the \(p\) coefficients when the weights are the constant \(c\). The REML estimate of a dispersion parameter therefore changes under a constant rescaling of the weights, and the ML estimate does not.

See also

statmod_equations() for the split, statmod_design() for the assembly, statmod() to fit it.

Examples

dd <- data.frame(y = rnorm(20), x = runif(20), z = runif(20))
spec <- statmod_spec(y ~ x | sigma ~ z,
                     distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd)

# The terms have one entry per parameter of the family, in the family's
# order.
names(spec@terms)
#> [1] "mu"    "sigma"
spec@equations
#> $mu
#> ~x
#> <environment: 0x55c318d5d440>
#> 
#> $sigma
#> ~z
#> <environment: 0x55c318d5d440>
#> 

# Unweighted, so the weights are ones.
c(n = spec@n_obs, total_weight = sum(spec@weights))
#>            n total_weight 
#>           20           20
